name: Water spinach
summary: How Filipino growers usually raise kangkong, either upland kangkong sown from seed on beds or water kangkong grown from cuttings in wet fields and ditches, and harvested in about a month. For backyard and small market growers who want the usual way and simple steps to harvest more often.
season: Kangkong grows all year in the lowlands. Upland kangkong from seed is planted in any month with water nearby and does very well in the hot dry months. In the rainy months it needs raised beds. Water kangkong in paddies, pond edges and ditches grows the whole year where the ground stays wet.
material: Upland kangkong is grown from seed, often soaked in water overnight before sowing so it comes up fast and even. Water kangkong is grown from stem cuttings about 20 to 30 cm long taken from healthy plants, sometimes stood in water for a week or so until roots show.
spacing: Upland: four rows on a 1 m bed, 20 cm between rows and hills, 2 to 3 seeds a hill. Some growers use two rows 30 by 30 cm, or sow thick lines for pulling. Water kangkong cuttings are set close together in rows in the mud.
water: Upland kangkong is watered every day by hand or hose, or by furrow on bigger farms. Water kangkong lives in wet ground with shallow water that is raised slowly as it grows.
fertilizer: Chicken or pig manure is the usual base, mixed into the beds before sowing, with a little complete fertilizer (14 14 14) and urea. Many growers add a little urea or manure tea after sowing and again after each cutting.
care: Daily watering, hand weeding in the first two weeks, light feeding after each cutting, and picking off caterpillars. Water kangkong fields are kept free of floating weeds.
harvest: Ready about three to four weeks after sowing or planting. Upland kangkong is pulled whole or cut so it regrows. Water kangkong is cut again and again for many months. Shoots are bundled, kept wet and shaded, and sold fresh the same day.

steps.title: Plow and harrow
steps.how: Plow and harrow two or three times about a week apart, 15 to 20 cm deep, to get fine, weed free soil.

steps.title: Make beds and put base fertilizer
steps.how: Form beds about 1 m wide. Mix chicken manure and a little complete fertilizer and urea into the bed and cover with soil.
steps.tip: For a bed 1 m by 20 m a common guide is a sack of chicken manure, 1 kg of 14 14 14 and about 4 kg of urea.

steps.title: Soak the seed
steps.how: Soak the seed in clean water overnight and drain it before sowing.

steps.title: Sow on the beds
steps.how: Drop 2 to 3 seeds a hill in four rows on the bed, 20 cm between rows and hills. Growers who sell whole plants often sow thicker in lines and pull them all at harvest.

steps.title: Water every day
steps.how: Water right after sowing and every day after that, in the morning or late afternoon. Kangkong grows fast only when the soil stays moist.

steps.title: Weed and top dress
steps.how: Pull the weeds while they are small and give a light side dressing of urea or manure tea along the rows.

steps.title: Check the leaves
steps.how: Look for caterpillars, whiteflies and aphids under the leaves, and for white rust spots. Remove badly hit plants.

steps.title: Bundle and keep wet
steps.how: Wash or wet the plants, tie them in bundles and keep them shaded and moist so they do not wilt before selling.

steps.title: Pull or cut the shoots
steps.how: Three to four weeks after sowing, pull whole plants or cut the shoots a few nodes above the soil so they sprout again for a second and third cutting.

watering.traditional: Upland kangkong from seed is watered every day, by watering can or hose on small beds and by furrow on bigger farms, from the day it is sown to the day it is pulled. It loves water more than most vegetables, so growers plant it close to a well, a pump or a canal.
watering.method: A watering can or a hose with a sprinkler head on small beds, furrows between the beds on bigger farms. Water in the early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Upland kangkong does well in the rainy months on raised beds with only a little watering on dry days. Without a pump in the dry season, keep a small bed near a well or a rain barrel, or grow water kangkong in a wet corner of the farm instead.
watering.dryseason: In the hot dry months water every day without fail, in the cool early morning or late afternoon, and twice on very hot days on sandy soil. Kangkong grows very fast in the dry months if water is there.
watering.wet: Use raised beds in the rainy months so the water drains between rains, and skip watering on wet days. Upland kangkong takes wet soil better than most vegetables, but beds that stay flooded rot the young plants.

schedule.often: Water right after sowing, then every morning or late afternoon
schedule.amount: Wet the bed well each time without washing the seed out
schedule.why: Soaked seed sprouts in a few days only if the bed stays moist.

schedule.often: Every day in the morning or late afternoon. On hot days on sandy soil water twice if the shoots droop
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the whole bed moist. Kangkong takes more water than pechay without harm, as long as the beds drain
schedule.why: Kangkong grows fast and tender only when the soil stays moist. Dry soil makes thin, tough stems.

schedule.often: Keep watering daily. Water the bed the day before pulling
schedule.why: Moist soil lets whole plants pull out cleanly, and full shoots stay fresh longer.

schedule.often: If you cut the shoots instead of pulling, go on watering every day
schedule.amount: The usual daily watering, with a light side dressing after each cutting
schedule.why: The cut base sprouts again for a second and third cutting only with steady water.

critical: The whole crop: kangkong is cut in three to four weeks and every dry day shows in tougher stems and smaller bundles.
The first days after sowing, until the seedlings are up.

signs.dry: Shoots droop and the leaves turn small and pale, the stems grow thin, hard and stringy, and the plants flower early.
signs.wet: Young seedlings rot at the base and yellow, and white rust spots spread faster under the leaves in soggy, crowded beds.

better: A drip line or a hose with a fine head gives every hill the same water and saves work in the dry months.
Mulch the beds with rice straw or rice hull to keep the soil moist and the leaves clean of splashed mud.

steps.title: Ready the wet field
steps.how: Clear weeds from a paddy, a pond edge or a ditch and work the mud soft. Keep only shallow water at first.

steps.title: Cut the stems
steps.how: Cut healthy stems about 20 to 30 cm long, each with several nodes.

parts.title: Pick the mother plants
parts.how: Take cuttings from a clean stand of water kangkong with thick green stems and no yellowing, rot or insect damage.

parts.title: Cut pieces with several nodes
parts.how: Cut stem pieces about 20 to 30 cm long, each with several nodes, since the roots come out at the nodes. Pull off the leaves on the lower part that will go into the mud.

parts.title: Root them in water if you have time
parts.how: Some growers stand the bundles in shallow water in the shade until short white roots show at the nodes, then plant. Rooted cuttings take hold faster in the field.

steps.title: Push the cuttings into the mud
steps.how: Press the lower nodes of each cutting into the soft mud, in rows, leaving the tips above the water.

steps.title: Raise the water slowly
steps.how: Young plants cannot take deep water, so raise the water level little by little as the vines spread.

steps.title: Weed and add manure
steps.how: Pull floating and creeping weeds and spread manure or a little urea when the water is low.

steps.title: Tie in bundles
steps.how: Tie the shoots in bundles, keep them wet and shaded and sell them the same day.

steps.title: First cutting
steps.how: About a month after planting, cut the young shoots, leaving the base and some nodes to regrow. Cut again each time the new shoots are long and tender.
steps.tip: Feed lightly after each cutting so the regrowth stays thick.

watering.traditional: Water kangkong grows in paddies, pond edges and ditches that stay wet, so it is never watered by hand: the grower controls the water level instead. The cuttings go into soft mud with only shallow water, and the water is raised slowly as the vines spread.
watering.method: The water level in the paddy, pond edge or ditch is raised and lowered with the field's own inlet and outlet or a small pump. No hand watering is needed.
watering.rainfed: Water kangkong is grown where the ground stays wet on its own, in low paddies, pond edges, ditches and creek sides. Where these dry up in summer, growers move the planting to the wettest spot or switch to upland kangkong on watered beds.
watering.dryseason: Keep the field flooded with shallow water through the dry months. Let in water from the canal, pond or pump whenever the mud starts to show and crack.
watering.wet: In the typhoon months keep a way to let water out, because a sudden deep flood can drown young plants or wash the stand away. Older stands handle high water better than new ones.

schedule.often: Keep the mud soft and wet while you clear the weeds
schedule.amount: Only shallow water or wet mud
schedule.why: Soft mud lets the cuttings be pushed in and hold.

schedule.often: Keep the mud wet with only shallow water, leaving the tips of the cuttings above the water
schedule.amount: Wet mud to a few cm of water
schedule.why: Young cuttings cannot stand deep water and drown or float away.

schedule.often: Raise the water little by little as the vines grow and cover the surface. Lower it for a day or two when you spread manure or urea
schedule.amount: Deeper as the plants grow, but always with the shoot tips above the water
schedule.why: Rising water keeps the stems long and tender, and low water while feeding keeps the fertilizer from washing away.

schedule.often: Keep the field wet the whole time and cut the new shoots each time they are long and tender
schedule.amount: The same water level as before the cutting
schedule.why: A stand kept wet and fed keeps giving shoots for many months.

critical: The first week after planting, when the water must stay shallow so the cuttings root and do not drown.
Any dry spell that lets the mud dry and crack: the stems turn hard and the stand weakens.

signs.dry: Mud shows and cracks, stems turn hard and stringy, and the leaves yellow and shrink.
signs.wet: Young cuttings sink under deep water, rot and float loose.

better: Keep the water shallow at first and raise it in steps as the vines spread, instead of flooding a new planting.
Lower the water for a day or two before feeding, then bring it back, so the manure or urea stays in the field.

mistakes: Sowing old seed without soaking, so the stand comes up thin and uneven.
Letting the beds dry out in hot months, which makes the stems tough.
Cutting too low on plants meant to regrow, leaving no nodes to sprout.
Flooding young water kangkong too deep before it has rooted.
Harvesting at midday and leaving bundles in the sun, so they wilt.
better: Buy fresh seed of a good upland variety, or take cuttings only from healthy, vigorous plants.
Test the soil and give balanced fertilizer instead of urea alone, which keeps leaves tender and safe to eat.
Use raised beds and mulch in the rainy months and water every day in the dry months.
Feed lightly after each cutting and plan cuttings so the bed keeps producing.
Scout weekly for caterpillars and white rust and remove sick plants early.
Grow water kangkong only in clean water, away from drains and dirty canals.
